The appellant, who was the sole executor of the will, claimed a declaration that the said document was the will of one G. Parthasarathy lyengar who was the owner of the properties mentioned in the schedule attached to the plaint. The appellant claimed a life interest in items 1 and 2 and the said properties as such were entitled to dispose of them by a will. The appellant 's case was that under the will the appellant was entitled to dispose them by a Will and that the will was not binding on him. The appellant contended that the will had been executed by G and that the appellant was not entitled to dispose it of by a will and that the properties were not liable to be disposed of by a Will. The trial court held that the will did not confer on G any right to dispose of the properties in question and that the said properties were not the subject matter of the will and that G had no right to dispose them of by a testamentary disposition. The High Court, however, held that the appellant had no right in the properties and that the respondent had no right of disposal of them by the will. The High court also held that the respondent was entitled to the properties in dispute. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the will could not be acted upon as it was not executed by G. The will was not a will and the appellant was bound to dispose of all the properties in accordance with the will. It was not a testamentary disposition and the will was a testamentary disposition within the meaning of section 68 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and was not binding upon the appellant. The will had been duly registered and the appellant had not been able to prove the will. Held, further, that the will executed by G was not a Will and the appellant could not be held to be entitled to the property in dispute. Held, also, that the appellant could be held to have no right to the properties. The will could not confer on the appellant any right to the property. The will did not create any interest in the properties. It was a testamentary arrangement and the appellant 's claim to the properties was not barred by section 68 of Act, 1925. The will executed by the appellant was a testamentary settlement and the appellant did not acquire any interest in them. The will, therefore, did not confer any right on G. The appellant was entitled only to the properties and not to the properties which were the subject matter in the will.

The appellants, who were manufacturers of electrical equipment, were assessed to sales tax under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957, on the ground that they were not liable to pay sales tax. The appellants contended that the sales were not liable for sales tax. They contended that the goods were not liable as they were not used for the purpose of the manufacture of electrical equipment. The High Court held that the appellants were not liable. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the sales of electrical equipment were not liable because they were not consumed for the purpose for which they were used. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: The High Court rightly held that the main use of the are carbons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in cinemas. The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that add to the beauty, convenience, or effectiveness of something else". [563 B C] The term "lamps" is used to describe goods, which may havebeen manufactured for use in cinemas. [563 C D] The term 'accessories ' is used in a sense in which they are used as an aid to the use of the equipment in the projectors or other cinematographic equipment. [564 D] The High Court correctly held that the primary use of the goods was duly proved by the appellants to be that they were that of production. [565 E]

The petitioners further contended that the impugned notifications were violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they were in the nature as they were not in the interest of mineral development. The power to make laws is subject to the provisions of the Constitution. The appellants, who were candidates for election to the Municipal Corporation of Raipur, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the electoral roll on the ground that the election to the Municipality was vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules, 1963. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was not justified in dismissing the petition on the ground of delay and laches. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts under Article 226 are not courts of appeal to entertain petitions under Article 226. The High courts are not courts to entertain petitions filed under Article 226, but are courts to exercise their jurisdiction judiciously and reasonably having regard to the surrounding circumstances. [515C] 2. The High court is not justified in entertaining the petition on account of delay in filing it. The High, Court was not right in dismissing the writ petition as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay in preferring it. [516C] 3. The High power under Article 226 is discretionary and if the High Court finds that there is not satisfactory explanation for delay, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue of writ will lead to public inconvenience and interference with rights of others. [517C] 4. The High Power under Article 226 does not ordinarily be discretionary and if it finds the delay in filing the petition should be ignored. [518C]

The plaintiffs and the defendant were adjoining colliery owners at Kujama. The plaintiffs ' land was leased to the respondent and the respondent leased it to the respondent on a reduced rent. The plaintiffs filed a suit for the recovery of the lease money and for the recovery thereof. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court held that the lease was not a lease but only a lease and that the plaintiffs were bound to keep a barrier of 25 feet to the south of the respondent 's working and, therefore, the coal that was still left in the encroached area was not by any means accessible to the plaintiffs and was entirely lost to them. The High Court also held that the plaintiffs had no knowledge of the appellant 's encroachment of their coal mines only in the year 1941 which was within three years of the date of the filing of the suit. The High court also held that under the Rules the appellants could not have asked for the exclusion of the respondent from the operation of the rule. The High, Court also held in favour of the respondent. The appellants came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the lease deed was not a licence but a lease and the plaintiffs were not bound to keep the same. The lease was not only a lease but also a lease and it was not a contract of lease. The lease deed was a lease and not a lease. The plaintiffs were bound by the rules and regulations made under the Indian Mines Act, 1923, and the Rules and Regulations made thereunder. The lease could not be said to be a lease. It was a lease. There was no evidence that the lease had been made by the lessee. The lease had been executed by the lessee in favour of his predecessor in interest. The lease did not contain any condition that the lessee should have been in possession of the land. The lease itself was not a transfer of the lease but was a lease of the land and the lessee was bound to keep it in the same condition as he was in possession. The lease in the present case was a lease, and the lease was a lease for the purpose of the lease. The lessee was not bound to maintain the lease and the lease could not have been created by the lessee without the consent of the lessor. The lease created a lease and was not a sale. The lease being a lease the lessee was not entitled to the benefit of the rule of the land, and the lessee could not be held to be bound by the lease.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, and was, at the material dates, in charge of certain works at a place called Karhali. He was also a Sub Divisional officer in charge of the Public Works department. He was charged with the offence of forging the thumb impression of the appellant and under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for forging the thumb impressions of the appellant. The trial Magistrate acquitted the appellant but the High Court, on appeal, held that the prosecution was not illegal, as sanction had not been obtained under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for his prosecution, and that the evidence on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate Court. Held, that the prosecution which had resulted in the conviction of the appellant was not competent to prosecute him under section 409, Indian Penal Code, and the conviction was illegal. The High Court, on appeal, maintained the conviction and sentence. The appellants contended that the presumption that they were dacoits was not drawn because the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, According to the appellants, the presumption to be drawn ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances do not admit the draw of such a result in the case. Held, that the presumption is not drawn because of the circumstances of the case. The presumption is not a rule of law but a rule of prudence. It is not a question of law but one of fact. The law is well settled that the presumption can be drawn only when the circumstances are such that the Court is satisfied that the accused was responsible for the crime. The presumption can be rebutted by the evidence of the circumstances which are not inconsistent with the innocence of the accused. The presumption cannot be drawn on the basis of the circumstances beyond his control. The presumption may be drawn from circumstances which are inconsistent with the guilt of the accused or from circumstances which create a reasonable doubt about the guilt of him. The presumption could be drawn only if the circumstances are inconsistent with his innocence. The presumption, however, must be one which the accused is able to prove. The accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt.

The appellants were the workmen of the respondent company. The Conciliation Officer wrote to the Conciliation Officer that no useful purpose would be served by holding any further meetings. The appellants appealed to this Court. Held, that the conciliation proceedings were not pending when the conciliation proceedings commenced and the conciliation proceedings concluded. The conciliation proceedings were commenced in the present case on the basis of the report of the Conciliation Officer. The conciliation proceeding was not commenced on the report of conciliation officer but on the basis that the conciliation proceeding was commenced on the basis the report of Conciliation Officer. Section 12(6), therefore, did not apply to the conciliation proceedings. The conciliation should be held to terminate when the Conciliation officer is required under section12(6) to submit his report. The conciliation must be held to have commenced on the date when the conciliation proceeding commenced and the report of such conciliation must be made and the proceedings closed. The conciliation, in the present ease, was commenced on January 17,, 1952, and the conciliation proceeding ended on the date of the commencement of the conciliation proceedings and the conciliation was commenced on March 18, 1952. The conciliation was commenced in the year 1952, and was completed on March 18. The conciliation in the presentcase was commenced on February 19, 1952, when the conciliation was completed on the basis, the report of a conciliation officer was received by the appropriate Government. The conciliation officer was not bound to make his report within 14 days but he was bound to make the report within 14 hours. The conciliation enquiry was commenced on April 15, 1952, but the conciliation proceedings ended on March 18 and the conciliation must be deemed to have concluded on March 18 on the date on which the conciliation proceedings was commenced. The conciliation would be deemed to commence when the report of an conciliation officer is received by the Central Government.

The appellants who were dealers in cotton and groundnuts were prosecuted under the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, for contravening the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder, and for contravention of the provisions of section 5(4)(a) of the Act. The appellants contended that the provisions of sections 5(4) (a) and (b) of the Madras Commercial crops Markets Act were void as they were not in the nature of trade allowance and were not in any transaction of sale of goods. Held, that the provisions contained in section 5(1) of the said Act were not void as they did not impose any tax or duty on the sale of goods and were not hit by article 19(6) of the Constitution. The Act was not a law relating to trade and commerce and was not saved by article 19 (6) of Constitution. The provisions of the Madras Act were not in terms of article 19(1)(g) of the constitution and were not saved by articles 19(6). The Act was a law relating only to trade and not to trade and was not protected by article 19. The Act did not impose a tax or duty or a duty on the transaction of sale or purchase of goods. The Act, therefore, was not saved under article 19(2) of the, Constitution. The question whether a particular payment was a trade allowance or not was a question of fact to be determined in each case. The question was not one of fact. The Act in the present case was not a taxing statute. The Act had no application to the facts of the case. The Act could not be said to be a law relating exclusively to trade and business. The Act being a law relating mainly to trade and the Act was not saved from article 19(5) of theConstitution. The Act having been passed for the purpose of preventing the commission of certain offences, it was not saved. The Act is not saved by the articles of the Constitution and the Act is not protected by articles 19 (6). The provisions of section 14 of the Act were not saved under articles 19 (1) (g) and 19 (6), and the Act could not therefore be saved under articles 14 and 19(6), as they were protected by articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution, as they were in the nature Of trade and not in the matter of trade and commerce.

The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The Sessions Judge acquitted the appellants but the High Court confirmed the sentence. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the appellants were not guilty of murder and the High Court was right in confirming the sentence. It was not correct to say that the appellants had been rightly convicted. The appellants were not convicted of murder and their conviction was not illegal. The appellants had been convicted of murder under section 302 and the sentence was reduced to imprisonment for life. The conviction was not correct. The conviction could not be sustained. The conviction of the appellants was not correct because the High Court had not considered the evidence on the record and the reasons given by the Sessions Judge for the conviction were not sufficient to justify the conviction. The conviction under section 302 was not correct and the High Courts were wrong in confirming the conviction.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of land in the village of Raikot in the same district in 1949. Their father, who was the appellant in the appeal, died and after his death, the application for review was dismissed by the Additional Custodian General. The appellants preferred a revision application before the Custodian General which was rejected. The appellants then moved the Custodian General for calling up their review application and for revising the order of the Additional Custodian cancelling the allotment of land. The Additional Custodian, however, dismissed the application on the ground that the cancellation was a result of misconception of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban land a had been wrongly fitted in the village Karodian. The appellants ' application for review of the order was also kept pending till the decision of the application of the 14 allottees of the village. The Additional Director of Administration, however, rejected the application on grounds that the allotment of the land in favour of the appellants was a result which was not permissible under the rules. The appellants filed a revision application to the Custodian General. During the pendency of the revision application the Additional Custodian, who was a party to the proceedings, was directed to dispose of the revision petition as expeditiously as possible. The Custodian General dismissed the revision application on the view that the order of cancellation of allotment of land was a result in misconception of the real facts and that the allotment had been wrongly made. The appellants came up to this Court by way of appeal by special leave. Held, that the order passed by the Additional Director of Estates was not a nullity and the order was not a final order. The order was not one of cancellation of the allotment of lands in favour of appellants. The order of the Custodian was not a decision of the Custodian General but was a decision of a Court of competent jurisdiction. The order could not be challenged in a revision petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The order passed by a Custodian was not one which was in conflict with the provisions of section 10 of the Act. The order did not affect the rights of the appellants. The Custodian had no power to cancel the allotment of a land in favour the appellants.
